items.readable_text:
Content:
Area models can be used to represent division problems.

Content:
For example, let's take a look at the following area model.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fc97af20c1010fa76cb86f4e827712d8]

Content:
Now, let's look at the big rectangle:

Content:
- its length is [MATH: 10+6=16]
- its width is [MATH: 4]
- its area is [MATH: {\color{blue}{40}}+{\color{blue}{24}}=64]

Content:
Since the area of the big rectangle equals its length multiplied by its width, this model represents the following multiplication problem:

Content:
[MATH: 16 \times 4= 64]

Content:
Writing this as a division problem, we get

Content:
[MATH: 16 = 64\div 4.]

Content:
Note: When using area models to represent division problems, the divisor ([MATH: 4] in this case) is the number on the left-hand side of our model.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Using Area Models to Represent Division Problems

Content:
Area models can be used to represent division problems.

Content:
For example, let's take a look at the following area model.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fc97af20c1010fa76cb86f4e827712d8]

Content:
Now, let's look at the big rectangle:

Content:
- its length is [MATH: 10+6=16]
- its width is [MATH: 4]
- its area is [MATH: {\color{blue}{40}}+{\color{blue}{24}}=64]

Content:
Since the area of the big rectangle equals its length multiplied by its width, this model represents the following multiplication problem:

Content:
[MATH: 16 \times 4= 64]

Content:
Writing this as a division problem, we get

Content:
[MATH: 16 = 64\div 4.]

Content:
Note: When using area models to represent division problems, the divisor ([MATH: 4] in this case) is the number on the left-hand side of our model.
